pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 10–11 years

- **Topic:** Nutrient Transport in Animals

- **Standards — UK (DfE Y6 'Animals, including humans'):** "describe the ways in which nutrients and water are transported within animals, including humans".

- **Standards — US (no direct NGSS PE at this band):** transport by the circulatory subsystem is treated at MS-LS1-3 (body as interacting subsystems); no US elementary PE. Treat as UK-led.

- **Operational details:** This topic JOINS two systems the child has met separately: digestion (which breaks food into nutrients) and circulation (which carries them). The organising idea is a DELIVERY NETWORK: food is digested → nutrients (and water) are absorbed into the blood at the small intestine → the heart pumps blood through vessels → nutrients and water (and oxygen) are delivered to every cell in the body, and waste is carried away. The key conceptual move is that the blood is a TRANSPORT system connecting digestion to the whole body — nutrients don't just 'stay in the gut', they travel in the blood to where they're needed. Keep it at whole-system level (absorb→carry→deliver); capillary-level diffusion detail is KS3.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier B (transitional, integrative). A Y6 child can describe each system alone; the target here is INTEGRATING them — tracing a nutrient from food, into the blood, and out to a working cell — which is the transitional, systems-thinking step.
bestPractices: Explicitly CONNECT the digestive and circulatory systems the child learned separately — this topic's whole value is the integration, so teach the hand-off at the small intestine.
Trace a concrete journey (a nutrient from a meal to a working cell) rather than describing transport abstractly, so the delivery network is followed step by step.
Stress that nutrients and water are ABSORBED INTO THE BLOOD and carried onward, correcting the idea that they stay in the gut.
Include water and oxygen as co-passengers and waste as the return cargo, so blood is understood as a two-way transport system.
Keep it whole-system (absorb→carry→deliver); defer capillary diffusion and active transport to KS3.
Use the correct vocabulary (blood vessels, artery/vein, nutrient, absorb) consolidated from the linked topics.
keyRepresentations: A linked digestive+circulatory diagram connected at the small intestine
A 'follow the nutrient' journey path from food → gut → blood → body cell
A close-up of nutrients/water crossing the intestine wall into a blood vessel
A whole-body delivery-network schematic (heart pumps, vessels branch, cells receive)
A two-way cargo diagram (nutrients/water/oxygen out, waste back)
commonMisconceptions: Thinking nutrients stay in the stomach or gut, rather than being absorbed into the blood and delivered around the body.
Treating digestion and circulation as unrelated systems, missing that circulation delivers what digestion releases.
Believing blood only carries oxygen, overlooking nutrients and water as cargo.
Assuming food 'becomes energy' directly in the gut, skipping the transport of nutrients to cells that then use them.
Thinking transport is one-way (delivery only), missing that blood also carries waste away from cells.

learn.summary: For ages 10–11 (UK DfE Y6 'Animals, including humans', statutory requirement to 'describe the ways in which nutrients and water are transported within animals, including humans'): the whole value of this topic is INTEGRATING two systems the child has met separately — digestion (breaks food into nutrients) and circulation (carries them). The organising idea is a delivery network: food is digested → nutrients and most water are absorbed into the blood at the small-intestine wall (the large intestine absorbs some more water) → the heart pumps blood through vessels → nutrients, water and oxygen are delivered to every cell, and waste is carried away. The key conceptual move is that nutrients do not stay in the gut — they travel in the blood to where they are needed. Keep it at whole-system level (absorb→carry→deliver); capillary diffusion and active transport are KS3.

activities.title: Follow one nutrient from a meal to a working cell
feedback: If a learner says food travels through tubes straight to the leg muscle, point to the small-intestine wall: nutrients are absorbed INTO the blood there; the blood, not the gut, delivers them to cells.
If a learner places absorption in the stomach, clarify that most absorption happens in the small intestine (its folded, villi-covered surface is huge); the stomach mainly digests.
If a learner treats the two systems as unconnected, highlight the handover point at the intestine wall: digestion prepares soluble nutrients, circulation distributes them.
If a learner thinks blood only carries oxygen, remind them nutrients and water are also cargo, and waste is the return load.
activities.rationale: Tracing one concrete journey step by step makes the absorb→carry→deliver network followable rather than abstract, and foregrounds the hand-off at the small intestine that is the actual integration target for this Tier B transitional checkpoint.
sourceClaims: For KS2: nutrients and water absorbed from digested food enter the blood and are carried by the circulatory system to cells throughout the body, linking the digestive and circulatory systems.
learnerActions: Pick a mouthful of food and trace what happens to it as it is digested along the gut.
At the small-intestine wall, identify the pivotal moment: the nutrient crosses OUT of the gut tube and INTO a blood vessel (absorption).
Follow the nutrient as the heart pumps blood carrying it through the vessels out to a working muscle cell (e.g. a leg muscle) that grabs and uses it.
Note the co-passengers — water and oxygen riding along in the blood too — and the waste picked up for the return trip, so blood is understood as two-way transport.
Name each hand-off aloud or in writing: digested in the gut → absorbed into blood at the small intestine → carried by the circulatory system → delivered to the cell.
activities.intendedInsight: The digestive and circulatory systems the child learned separately are one connected delivery network: the food you eat is absorbed into the blood and travels to every cell in your body.

activities.title: Trace the journey on a body outline
feedback: If the traced line skips from gut straight to muscle, ask where the nutrient entered the blood — the path must cross the small-intestine wall into a vessel first.
If no return path is drawn, prompt: what happens to the waste the cell produces? Blood carries it away too.
activities.rationale: Constructing and verbalising the route (rather than selecting from options) elicits independent explanation and surfaces whether the learner can locate the absorption hand-off; recognition tasks alone do not elicit this production.
sourceClaims: For KS2: nutrients and water absorbed from digested food enter the blood and are carried by the circulatory system to cells throughout the body, linking the digestive and circulatory systems.
learnerActions: On a body outline, draw a meal in the gut and a target muscle (e.g. in the leg or toes).
Use a finger or a drawn/coloured line to trace the path from the drawn meal, through the gut, across the small-intestine wall into a blood vessel, through the pumping heart, and out to the muscle.
Narrate each hand-off between systems as you go ('here it's absorbed into the blood', 'here the heart pumps it on', 'here the cell uses it').
Add arrows showing waste returning from the cell back into the blood to show two-way transport.
activities.intendedInsight: Drawing and narrating the whole path on a body makes the delivery network a route the learner can reconstruct and explain, not just recognise.

activities.title: Explain the diagnostic 'how do nutrients reach a leg muscle?' question
feedback: A complete explanation says: digested nutrients are absorbed through the small-intestine wall into the blood; the circulatory system then carries the dissolved nutrients to every cell, including the leg muscle. The gut absorbs, the blood transports — they work together.
If the learner describes food reaching the leg through pipes with no absorption into blood, reteach the hand-off at the small intestine explicitly.
If the learner is vague about where absorption happens, point to the small intestine and its villi/surface area; the stomach mainly digests.

A vague answer that knows blood carries nutrients but cannot say where absorption happens or how the systems connect needs the absorption hand-off made explicit before it counts as a full explanation.
activities.rationale: A two-tier question that contrasts a tube-only story with the absorption-into-blood route discriminates genuine systems integration from surface recall and directly targets the known misconceptions.
learnerActions: Consider: after you digest your dinner, nutrients need to reach a muscle in your leg. A student says the food just travels down through your intestines and straight into the leg.
Explain how the nutrients actually get from gut to leg muscle: what carries them, and where do they cross over?

Answer the probing follow-ups: At which organ do nutrients pass out of the gut into the blood? Why does it help that the small intestine has a huge, folded inner surface? If the circulatory system stopped, why would a leg muscle starve even though there's food in the gut? How do the digestive and circulatory systems depend on each other to nourish a cell?
activities.intendedInsight: A learner who understands transport routes nutrients via absorption into the blood; one without it imagines food travelling bodily through the gut to its destination, with no role for blood.

constraints: Keep it whole-system (absorb→carry→deliver); defer capillary-level diffusion and active transport to KS3.
Use correct vocabulary consolidated from the linked topics: blood vessels, artery/vein, nutrient, absorb.

Address the core misconceptions directly: nutrients do not stay in the stomach/gut; blood carries nutrients and water (not just oxygen); food does not 'become energy' in the gut — nutrients are transported to cells that then use them; transport is two-way (waste returns).

An ordering/matching/multiple-choice check can consolidate the integrated pathway and is a useful assessment, but recognition-only responses do not themselves elicit the independent explanation that tracing and narrating a journey do; pair recognition checks with a construction task to build and show understanding.

A static labelled figure (gut connected to blood, tappable stages revealing 'absorbed here' / 'carried in blood' / 'delivered to cells', with myth-buster flaps like 'do nutrients stay in your tummy?') can teach the network and is a strong scaffold; it shows the linked systems rather than letting the learner trace the journey themselves, so pair it with a tracing or narration task.

An in-role framing ('be a nutrient' / 'interview a red blood cell about its delivery route') can motivate the journey narrative; keep it anchored to the actual anatomical route so the integration objective is met.

Interactive affordances (glowing particle crossing, learner-pumped heart, split connected-systems view, tappable stages, flaps) are optional ways to make the mechanism concrete, not required mechanisms; a finger-trace or drawn path can serve the same integration goal.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of a saved teaching-research row without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The source labels one interactive format 'ideal' and claims the particle-crossing is felt 'in a way no static image can'; this comparative-necessity claim is not established by the cited sources. It has been softened to a concrete tracing activity (which may be realised as an interactive, finger-trace, or drawn path) with the static-figure alternative preserved as a strong scaffold rather than an inferior option.
The source rates 3D as 'poor' because the network is flow-based; this is a format preference, not an established pedagogical law, and has been dropped rather than asserted as a universal limitation.

Two of three cited sources are marked verified:false in the source row (BBC Bitesize and NGSS); the DfE statutory requirement is the only verified claim. The DfE requirement is carried as objective context in the summary rather than cited as pedagogical support, because it establishes the curriculum topic, not the teaching principle behind these activities.

The BBC Bitesize claim is cited on the first two activities because it describes the absorb→carry→deliver content and the absorption hand-off those activities trace; it is not evidence that the tracing/narration method is more effective than other media, which remains untested.

Interactive affordances mentioned in the source (glowing particle, learner-pumped heart, split view of the two systems, tappable stages, myth-buster flaps) are preserved as OPTIONAL concreteness, not mandatory mechanisms.

probeDeeper: At which organ do the nutrients actually pass out of the gut and into the blood?
Why does it make sense that the small intestine has a huge, folded inner surface?
If the circulatory system stopped, why would a leg muscle starve even though there's food in the gut?
How do the digestive and circulatory systems depend on each other to nourish a cell?
assess.correctAnswer: The digested nutrients are absorbed through the wall of the small intestine into the blood; the circulatory system then carries the dissolved nutrients in the blood to every cell, including the leg muscle. The digestive and circulatory systems work together — the gut absorbs, the blood transports.

errorPatterns.pattern: Food travels through the gut and tubes straight to where it's needed
errorPatterns.nextMove: Nutrients are absorbed into the blood at the small intestine wall; the blood, not the gut, delivers them to cells. Link the two systems explicitly.
errorPatterns.distractor: The food travels through tubes straight to the leg muscle.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Describes food reaching the leg through pipes, with no absorption into blood

errorPatterns.pattern: Nutrients are absorbed in the stomach
errorPatterns.nextMove: Most absorption is in the small intestine, whose villi give a huge surface area; the stomach mainly digests, not absorbs.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Places absorption into the blood in the stomach rather than the small intestine

errorPatterns.pattern: The digestive and circulatory systems are completely separate
errorPatterns.nextMove: They interface at the intestine wall: digestion prepares soluble nutrients, and circulation distributes them. Show the handover point.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Treats the two systems as unconnected and can't say where they meet

responseLevels.gap: Imagines food travelling through the gut directly to its destination; no role for blood or absorption.
responseLevels.full: Explains nutrients are absorbed through the small-intestine wall into the blood and carried by the circulatory system to all cells, describing the two systems working together.
responseLevels.partial: Knows blood carries nutrients but is vague about where absorption happens or how the two systems connect.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: After you digest your dinner, the nutrients need to reach a muscle in your leg. A student says the food just travels down through your intestines and somehow straight into the leg. How do the nutrients actually get from your gut to a leg muscle — what carries them, and where do they cross over?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who understands transport routes nutrients via absorption into the blood. A child without it imagines food travelling bodily through the gut to its destination, with no role for blood.
